text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementNeuroscienceWhy Story and Playtime Really MatterFace-to-face interaction trumps screens for social and language learningKFBy Kristen French1:00 PM CDT on October 15, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleWhen baby needs watching and mom and dad get busy, the blue light of a glowing rectangle often beckons. Instead of playing another round of peek-a-boo while dinner burns, they may turn to a phone, iPad, or television to serve as a babysitter. Most babies now get screen time daily, according to recent data from the United Kingdom, with the average hovering around 41 minutes a day for 9-month-olds.What does this screen time do to their tender, developing brains? Infants are thought to learn best by doing, particularly when it comes to language and social skills. They rely heavily on face-to-face interaction, shared attention, and live conversational feedback with an adult caregiver, decades of evidence suggests. Differences in social engagement abilities are also a major feature of autism spectrum disorder, and deficits in this arena have been associated with slowed language development. Read more: “For Kids, Learning Is Moving”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
